messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Erin is a 38-year-old bartender who came to treatment months after her boyfriend was critically injured in a late-night assault outside the bar where she works. The night is fixed in her mind in flashes that still feel almost present tense: the bright spill of the neon beer sign on wet pavement, his face turning toward her when voices rose behind them, the sudden movement, blood on his shirt that looked too dark at first under the streetlight. She can describe those pieces with unnerving precision, as if they are snapshots she is forced to look at again and again. At the same time, there are stretches she cannot account for at all. She knows she screamed for help, and someone must have called 911, but the sequence between seeing him fall and finding herself in the emergency department corridor remains blank. What stands out to her most are images rather than a continuous story, and because those fragments are so sharp while the missing parts stay inaccessible, she has come to treat the gaps as evidence that she failed him in some crucial way.

In the weeks after the assault, Erin’s mind kept returning to the clearest moments, and she replayed them looking for what she should have done differently. She had urged her boyfriend to stay for one more drink after closing, and she had stepped back inside for her bag just before the confrontation began. She had come to believe the attack happened because of the way she acted, that if she had left sooner or stayed beside him continuously, none of it would have happened. The vividness of the images seemed, to her, to prove that these were the important moments she was supposed to have prevented. The blank patches did not soften that conviction; if anything, they made it worse. She was certain that if she could remember the missing minutes, they would show some additional mistake. As that belief hardened, it spread outward into a broader mistrust. She found herself thinking that people were not what they seemed, that danger could surface from ordinary faces without warning, and that relying on anyone else was how people got hurt.

Those beliefs shaped how she tried to get through each day. Erin began avoiding news reports about assaults, hospital stories, or any segment about random violence, switching channels or leaving the room before details could begin. She told herself there was no point in taking in more examples of what people were capable of. She also worked hard to keep a lid on any feeling that threatened to break through. During her shifts, if a customer’s raised voice or the scrape of shoes outside the front door brought up one of those frozen images, she would straighten glasses, focus on receipts, and clamp down on any sign of panic or grief. She has not sought medical or psychological help until now, in part because she does not believe other people can really be counted on, and in part because asking for help feels to her like handing control to someone who might fail her the way she believes she failed her boyfriend.

The bar itself has become one of the places where the problem is most visible. Near closing time, when the lighting changes and patrons drift out in uneven clusters, she is pulled back by specific visual fragments from that night. A man in a dark jacket pausing under the beer sign, a smear of red cocktail on the counter, an ambulance siren passing outside can bring the memory up in pictures so immediate that for a moment she feels pinned inside them. Those moments make her even more guarded. She watches customers closely, assumes friendliness can turn without warning, and avoids leaning on the bouncer or her coworkers even when they offer to walk her to her car. The memories leave her feeling that only constant self-control keeps things from getting worse, so she doubles down on staying composed and refusing help.

Over time, those strategies have fed back into the way she sees herself and other people. Because she avoids reminders in the news and has stayed away from medical and psychological settings, nothing has challenged her conviction that the world is fundamentally deceptive and that she alone is responsible for preventing disaster. Because she spends so much effort suppressing emotion, she experiences any crack in that control as further proof that she is not handling this well enough. She has become more distant with her boyfriend since his physical recovery, not because she cares less, but because she cannot bear to hear his version of the night or risk learning that he blames her too. What finally brought her in was a recent shift when a customer collapsed after being cut on broken glass and, before anyone even knew the injury was minor, Erin felt the old images slam back so clearly that she had to retreat to the stockroom. She is seeking help now because she is frightened that her life has narrowed to vigilance, silence, and self-blame, and because some part of her still hopes there may be a way to remember what happened without feeling condemned by it.
